name: Yusuf Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a freelance Arabic to English interpreter and translator, mostly legal work. Two or three days a week I'm at the county court or a solicitor's office, interpreting for people in housing cases, asylum appeals, sometimes a custody hearing. The rest of the week I translate witness statements and tenancy papers from my spare room. I like that the work matters, and I hate the waiting around in court corridors that nobody pays you for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. For a long tenancy agreement I'll sometimes run a rough first pass through a translation tool and then rewrite almost all of it, which saves me maybe an hour. I'd never use it for a witness statement, because one wrong word there and someone's case falls apart. Hana, my partner, teaches at a primary school and laughs that I trust a nine-year-old's spelling more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, legal language is full of traps that a machine falls into. I'd probably share an article about it in the interpreters' network chat. Mostly I'd say the real problem was never AI, it's the courts paying interpreters late and badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on, which is fine but not great. Legal aid rates haven't gone up in four years, and the court booking firm takes a big cut. With about four months of savings I'm okay, but I'm not getting ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the court work and use the translation tool for a few more of the boring tenancy jobs, to buy back some evenings. I'd also go to the union branch meeting about legal aid rates, which I've skipped twice. Maybe put a bit more into savings, since nothing's changing anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, with a little annoyance. The same frustrations as now, just without a robot to blame them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the court booking firm. What does it actually take from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm, Linguaserve, takes about a third of what the court pays for each hearing. If a hearing gets cancelled the morning of, I get nothing, even after travelling an hour. Linguaserve (the firm that books court interpreters) has done more damage to my pay than any AI ever has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older interpreters who still fax things, honestly. Some of them are booked less because the courts want everything digital now. That's not AI, that's just paperwork moving on, and it still pushes people out.

say: Legal language is **full of traps** that machines fall into, so I'm not surprised.
The real problem is courts and **booking firms paying** interpreters late and badly.
think: My life carries on, but **legal aid rates** haven't risen in four years.
**Four months of savings** keeps me okay, but I'm not getting ahead.
do: **Use the translation tool** on more routine tenancy jobs to win back evenings.
**Attend the union branch** meeting on legal aid rates he skipped twice.
**Add a bit more** to savings each month while things are steady.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with the usual annoyance about pay and cancelled hearings.
S0.quote: Linguaserve (the firm that books court interpreters) has done more damage to my pay than any AI ever has.
fieldNote: He blames **booking firms**, not technology, for his money worries.
Uses AI **pragmatically** for low-stakes text, but draws a hard line at witness statements.
His job feels **safe enough**, but stalled pay keeps it on his mind.

steps.text: Keep the two or three court days a week
Run routine tenancy papers through the translation tool first
Go to the union branch meeting on legal aid rates
Raise monthly savings while work stays steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say in public that legal interpreting has to stay human, because a person's freedom can turn on one word. I'd be pushing that line in the union and with the law society. I'd also say translators need help to adapt, not a pat on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the document side drops by half within a few years. Solicitors will run tenancy papers through software and only pay me to check the hard bits. Court interpreting holds longer, because judges are cautious, but the rates will get squeezed by the cheap option sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a proper course in using the translation tools for legal checking, because if checking's the job I want to be the best at it. I'd also apply for the court interpreter register at the higher tier, which takes an exam and about six months. And I'd stop eating lunch out in court and bring sandwiches, small stuff, to keep savings building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. It's not the end, but it's the end of the version of this job I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be learning the tools that cut your document work. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest, but I've seen this before with my dad. My dad was a typesetter who refused computers and ended up stacking shelves at fifty. I'd rather be the person checking the machine than the person replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana would say I'm overthinking it, then quietly work out our budget on a spreadsheet. Her teaching job is steady in this picture, so we'd be fine on rent. It just means I'd stop being the one who earns a bit more.

say: Legal interpreting must **stay human**, because one word can decide someone's freedom.
Translators need **real help to adapt**, not just encouragement.
think: **Document work halves** within a few years as solicitors use software.
Court interpreting lasts longer, but **rates get squeezed** by the cheap option.
do: **Take a course** in checking machine translation for legal work.
**Sit the exam** for the higher-tier court interpreter register within six months.
**Bring lunch to court** and keep building savings.
feel: **Uneasy and sad**, losing the version of the job he trained for.
S1.quote: My dad was a typesetter who refused computers and ended up stacking shelves at fifty.
fieldNote: His **father's story** drives his choice to learn the tools rather than resist.
He expects **half his document income** to go, which makes this anxious, not uneasy.
Partner's **steady teaching job** is the household's safety net.

steps.text: Take a course in checking machine legal translation
Sit the higher-tier court interpreter register exam
Bring packed lunches to court instead of buying
Push the union and law society to keep court interpreting human

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless and someone needs to slow it down, and I'd sign every petition going. I'd say the courts can't just switch to machines for asylum hearings without a law saying so. Online I'd probably be angrier than I am in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think by 2028 most of my work is gone, court included. The whole job is thinking and talking, so the robots coming later makes no difference to me. The only question is whether a law keeps a human in court for a few extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first months saving every penny I could and taking every hearing on offer. I'd ask Hana's school about teaching assistant roles for Arabic-speaking children, because that's work with people in a room. And I'd go to the union to push for a law that keeps humans in court interpreting, because that's my only real shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with a tight chest. Two years is no time to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at teaching assistant work. Would that pay the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, about two thirds of what I make now, maybe less. But it's a room full of children who need someone, and I can't see a machine doing that in two years. We'd have to cut back on the holiday we'd planned and stop thinking about moving to a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at court would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clients, more than the interpreters. A frightened man in an asylum appeal listening to a machine voice explain his case is not progress, just cheaper. I'd say that to any judge who asked.

say: This is **reckless**, and someone needs to **slow it down**.
Courts can't switch asylum hearings to machines **without a law**.
think: By 2028 most of my work is **gone, court included**.
My job is **all thinking work**, so the later robots change nothing for me.
do: **Take every hearing** offered and save hard in the first months.
**Ask about teaching assistant** roles supporting Arabic-speaking children.
**Push the union** for a law keeping humans in court interpreting.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a tight chest, because two years is too short to start over.
S2.quote: A frightened man in an asylum appeal listening to a machine voice explain his case is not progress, just cheaper.
fieldNote: He sees **no robot delay** for himself, since interpreting is all thinking work.
Plans a **pay cut** to teaching assistant work and delayed housing plans.
His concern shifts quickly to **vulnerable clients**, which grounds his politics.

steps.text: Save every spare penny and take every hearing in the first months
Apply for teaching assistant roles supporting Arabic-speaking pupils
Campaign through the union for human-only court interpreting
Drop the plan to move to a bigger flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to pass a law, so pass it. I'd be on the panels and the union calls, saying courts and hospitals should keep human interpreters. I'd also say we need a retraining wage, not just free online courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my work around 2030 or 2031. Five years gives me time to get a teaching qualification, which is the thing I keep coming back to. I'd be thirty-two, and Hana and I might be thinking about kids by then, so it matters a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply to do a teaching qualification part time, maybe teaching English as an additional language. I'd keep the court work going three days a week to pay for it. I'd also push Linguaserve and the union to agree fair rates for checking machine work while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busier than scared. There's a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make us wait until I'm qualified, probably. I wouldn't want a baby arriving the same year my income disappears. Hana would say that's sensible and also a bit sad, and she'd be right on both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose the work around 2031 but you sound fairly steady. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'd lose this job, that I'm sure of. But I'd have a different job lined up, so the fear is about the gap, not the end.

say: **Five years** is time enough to pass a law, so pass it.
We need a **retraining wage**, not just free online courses.
think: Five years gives me time for a **teaching qualification** before kids.
do: **Apply for a teaching** course in English as an additional language, part time.
**Keep court work** three days a week to pay for the course.
**Push for fair rates** on machine-checking work while it lasts.
feel: **Anxious but busy**, steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want a baby arriving the same year my income disappears.
fieldNote: He is **sure he loses** this job, so his mood stays high despite a plan.
**Family timing** is the real stake: kids wait until he's qualified.
The gap he fears is **between jobs**, not the end of interpreting itself.

steps.text: Start a part-time course to teach English as an additional language
Keep court interpreting three days a week to fund the course
Negotiate fair machine-checking rates through the union
Wait to try for a baby until the teaching job starts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and it would be shameful to waste it. I'd want the union and government to plan for interpreters now, not in year nine. I'd say that sort of thing on a panel, and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could do most of my thirties in this job and still move on. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, which is a normal age to change careers. The worry is that the rates shrink long before the job officially ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep interpreting full time for the next couple of years and use the tools more for documents. Around year three I'd start the teaching course, so I'm qualified well before 2036. And I'd try to push savings from four months to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still a bit sad, but it feels like something I could live through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rates shrink before the job ends. When would you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the solicitors start asking for 'review only' on everything, which is already starting a little. When most of my emails from solicitors say review only, I'll know my interpreting days are numbered. I'd tell Hana and start the course early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at home with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for kids in a couple of years. Ten years is long enough that I wouldn't put our life on hold. I'd just make sure the savings were there first.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and wasting it would be shameful.
Unions and government should **plan for interpreters now**, not in year nine.
think: I could spend most of my **thirties interpreting** and still move on at thirty-seven.
**Rates will shrink** long before the job officially ends.
do: **Keep interpreting** full time and use the tools more for documents.
**Start the teaching course** around year three.
**Grow savings** from four months to six.
feel: **Steadier**, though a little sad, as if this is survivable.
S4.quote: When most of my emails from solicitors say review only, I'll know my interpreting days are numbered.
fieldNote: He has a **clear signal** for when to move: review-only requests from solicitors.
**Family plans** go ahead, but only once savings are in place.
Still expects to **lose the job**, so anxious, though with a lot of control.

steps.text: Keep interpreting full time for the next two years
Use translation tools on more document jobs
Start the teaching course around year three
Build savings from four months to six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years doesn't give me time to qualify for anything. What would help is a law that keeps human interpreters in courts for a set number of years, and a wage while people like me retrain as teachers. Free courses don't pay rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what clients think. I've sat next to people who'd waited years for their day in court. A man waiting three years for his asylum hearing wants to look at a person, not a speaker on a table.

headlineQuote: A man waiting three years for his asylum hearing wants to look at a person, not a speaker on a table.
portrait: A **27-year-old freelance** Arabic to English legal interpreter who works courts and solicitors' offices.
Uses **translation tools** now and then for routine documents, but never for witness statements.
Blames **booking firms** and legal aid rates more than AI for his money worries.
His **father's lost trade** pushes him to learn the tools and plan a move into teaching.
Times **having children** around how fast interpreting work disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to qualify for anything new.
whatWouldHelp: A law keeping **human court interpreters** for a set number of years.
A **wage while retraining** as a teacher, since free courses don't pay rent.
